title: Sultanate of Gowa
capsule: The Sultanate of Gowa was a Makassarese maritime state in South Sulawesi, traditionally founded c. 1300 and, by the early seventeenth century, the dominant power controlling much of the eastern Indonesian spice trade from its capital at Sombaopu. The ruling dynasty converted to Islam on 22 September 1605 under Sultan Alauddin, then prosecuted Islamic wars from 1611 that brought neighbouring kingdoms including Bone under its suzerainty. Sultan Hasanuddin (r. 1653–1669) led determined resistance against the Dutch VOC and its Bugis ally Arung Palakka; after the VOC stormed Sombaopu on 12 June 1669, the Treaty of Bungaya stripped Gowa of its commercial empire and Fort Rotterdam was built on the ruins of its harbour fortress.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The sultanate's core territory in South Sulawesi and its suzerain reach are documented in Dutch VOC records and Makassarese lontaraq chronicles; peripheral tributary boundaries are imprecise.
